summary: A 1976 proposal for the Message Services Data Transmission Protocol, a mechanism for message servers to move data between hosts. It treats the process as a translation between abstract items such as strings and integers and the byte formats that represent them.

eli5.summary: Two computers need to send things like words and numbers in a shared form. This note describes a way to pack and unpack them.

subtitle: A common way for message servers to encode and transmit data structures

tldr.problem: Message servers transferring data between computers with different internal representations must translate abstract concepts like integers and strings to a common byte format. Each system would define translation rules independently, limiting compatibility.
tldr.mechanism: MSDTP defines primitive data items (integers, character strings, bit streams, booleans), the rules for extending them with application-specific semantic items, and a set of byte-stream objects that encode these items. Translation rules map between abstract items known to programmers and physical byte formats.
tldr.outcome: MSDTP influenced the thinking about data serialization and was used in some message systems, but the specific format did not become a widespread standard. Later protocols adopted similar layered approaches to data representation.

today: RFC 713 is a design for structured data serialization for message systems. Though MSDTP itself was not standardized widely, the concept of separating abstract data definitions from wire formats influenced later serialization standards such as ASN.1 and similar protocols.

sections.title: Data Translation Between Systems
sections.content:
RFC 713 addresses a fundamental challenge when programs on different computers exchange data: each system represents integers, strings, and other types differently in memory. An MSDTP (Message Services Data Transmission Protocol) acts as a translator. Programmers define data using high-level items (for example, p-INT for an integer or p-STRING for a character string). The MSDTP encodes these items into a standard byte format for transmission, and the receiver decodes the bytes back into local representations.

The protocol separates the concept from the representation: programmers work with abstract items, the protocol handles byte encodings, and the translation machinery is the same everywhere. This lets programs exchange data without worrying about the differences between the machines involved.
sections.eli5: You write your code using familiar numbers and words. The protocol translates them to a standard format for travel and back again at the destination. Like a translator who knows both languages.

sections.title: Items, Objects, and Encoding
sections.content:
The protocol defines primitive items: p-INT (integers), p-STRING (strings), p-BITS (bit streams), p-CHAR (single characters), p-BOOL (true or false), p-STRUC (grouped data), p-EMPTY (placeholder for no data), and p-XTRA (application-defined single-byte items). Systems can define semantic items for application-specific data like dates or file specifications by tagging them with a type code and version number.

The protocol then defines byte-stream objects (prefixed b-) that encode these items. Each object begins with a type byte that specifies what kind of data follows. Atomic objects efficiently encode common data; non-atomic objects handle larger or less common items. The type byte and following bytes are sufficient for a decoder to reconstruct the original item.
sections.eli5: You can send plain things like numbers and text, but also invent your own thing if you label it. The protocol packs these into bytes in a way that any program can unpack and understand.

sections.title: Application Integration
sections.content:
A site implementing MSDTP provides encoding and decoding functions. Applications define their interactions using items, without concern for representation details. A message server uses the MSDTP to translate between its internal data structures and the byte format sent over the network. This decouples applications from the transport layer and lets them use higher-level concepts.

Semantic items extend the protocol for application-specific needs. A message system might define a FILE semantic item carrying a host number and pathname. These are encoded as extended data types (tagged structures) and decoded back to semantic items at the receiver, preserving meaning across different systems.
sections.eli5: Programs just say what data they want to send using the protocol's vocabulary. The protocol does the packing and unpacking, so programmers can focus on what the data means, not how to format it.
